common_name: Silver Queen Rex Begonia (Heirloom Silver-Leaf Rhizomatous Begonia)

planting.note: Divide and repot rhizome sections in spring as new growth resumes, moving plants outdoors to shade only once nights stay above 55 degrees F.

directions: Silver Queen is one of the oldest named Rex begonia cultivars still in general cultivation, grown for broad, asymmetrically heart-shaped leaves whose surface is washed almost entirely in metallic silver, leaving only a thin band of dark green tracing the veins and leaf margin. Pot it shallowly in a fast-draining, humus-rich mix, since the creeping surface rhizome quickly rots if kept constantly wet, and set it in bright, indirect light that intensifies the silvery sheen without scorching the thin leaf blades. Humidity above 50 percent keeps the leaf edges from crisping in dry indoor air, so group it with other rhizomatous begonias or set the pot on a pebble tray. Propagate by dividing congested rhizomes at repotting time or by rooting leaf-wedge cuttings in moist peat.

planting.note: Start tubers indoors in warmth after danger of frost has passed, since this hybrid has essentially no cold tolerance outside tropical and subtropical zones.

directions: Kimjongilhwa, meaning 'Kim Jong Il flower,' is a red-flowered begonia hybrid created in 1988 by Japanese horticulturist Kamo Mototeru and dedicated to the North Korean leader, where it is propagated at a dedicated greenhouse complex outside Pyongyang and displayed each February during the Day of the Shining Star festival alongside the red orchid Kimilsungia. It produces clusters of large, glossy, deep-red blooms held above compact, fleshy-stemmed foliage and continues flowering over an extended season when kept warm and humid. Grow it in bright, indirect light with consistent warmth and even moisture, letting the surface of the growing medium dry slightly between waterings to protect the fleshy roots from rot. It has essentially no frost tolerance, so outside tropical climates it is maintained strictly as a container or greenhouse specimen.

planting.note: Divide the spreading rhizome into sections with at least one growing point in spring and pot into a wide, shallow container.

directions: Marmaduke is a large-growing rhizomatous begonia selected for its oversized, quilted leaves, which emerge deep bronze-green dusted with silvery overtones across a puckered surface and deepen in color as they mature. Its thick, creeping rhizome stores considerable water and energy, so the growing medium should be allowed to dry noticeably at the surface between waterings even though the broad leaves wilt dramatically if left dry too long. Grow it in bright, indirect light in a wide, shallow container that can accommodate the spreading rhizome, dividing congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor and produce new starts. Its substantial scale makes it a strong textural anchor among shade-garden containers or in a collection of smaller rhizomatous begonias.

planting.note: Divide congested rhizome clumps in spring and repot into shallow containers of fast-draining mix.

directions: Potpourri takes its name from the jumbled mix of colors splashed across each leaf, where patches of bronze, green, silver, and deep maroon blend unevenly over a rounded, puckered surface so that no two leaves look quite alike. Like other rhizomatous begonias in the American Begonia Society tradition, it spreads by a creeping surface rhizome best grown in a shallow pot of fast-draining, peat-based mix kept on the dry side between waterings. Bright, indirect light brings out the strongest color contrast in the mottling, while deeper shade causes the leaves to green over and lose their patterned effect. Propagate by rhizome division at repotting time or by rooting a leaf-petiole cutting in moist medium to raise new plants true to the parent's leaf pattern.

common_name: Solenia Dark Pink Begonia (Compact Rose-Double Tuberous Begonia)

planting.note: Set out rooted plants or started tubers after all danger of frost has passed into containers or hanging baskets.

directions: Solenia Dark Pink is part of a cutting-propagated tuberous begonia series bred for continuous, weather-resistant flowering, producing fully double, rose-form blooms in a rich dark pink that hold their shape and color through rain and heat far better than older seed-grown tuberous begonias. Its compact, well-branched habit and glossy, deep-green foliage keep the plant tidy in containers and hanging baskets without the leggy stretch typical of some tuberous types. Grow in a rich, well-drained potting mix in bright, indirect light to gentle morning sun, keeping the soil evenly moist but never waterlogged, since the fleshy stems and small tubers are prone to rot in soggy conditions. Deadheading is unnecessary since spent flowers drop cleanly, but pinching young growth encourages a fuller, more floriferous plant.

common_name: Million Kisses Elegance Begonia (Trailing Apricot-Orange Begonia)

planting.note: Plant started tubers or rooted cuttings into hanging baskets after frost danger has passed, pinching young stems to encourage branching.

directions: Million Kisses Elegance is a trailing tuberous begonia bred from Begonia boliviensis lines, producing long, gracefully arching stems lined with narrow, bright orange-red, bell-shaped flowers that hang like a continuous curtain of blooms from early summer through frost. Its naturally cascading habit, far more pendulous than bedding-type tuberous begonias, makes it especially suited to hanging baskets and tall containers where the trailing stems can drape freely. Grow in rich, well-drained, consistently moist potting mix in bright, indirect light to a few hours of gentle morning sun, since too much shade reduces flowering while harsh afternoon sun scorches the thin leaves. Pinch stem tips early in the season to encourage branching, and bring the tuber or a rooted cutting indoors before frost where winters are not reliably mild.

common_name: Pink Shadows Rex Begonia (Silver-Pink Overlay Rhizomatous Begonia)

planting.note: Divide the rhizome in spring and pot into shallow containers of fast-draining, peat-based mix.

directions: Pink Shadows is a Rex begonia cultivar grown for its heavily textured, puckered leaves, where a soft pink overlay spreads across a darker green-to-bronze base in an uneven, shadow-like pattern that shifts with the light. Pot it shallowly in a fast-draining, humus-rich mix and give it bright, indirect light, since the pink pigmentation intensifies with good light but the thin leaves scorch quickly in direct sun. Allow the surface of the mix to dry between waterings to protect the shallow rhizome from rot, and maintain humidity above 50 percent to prevent crisped leaf margins indoors. Divide the rhizome or root leaf-wedge cuttings at repotting time to propagate new plants.

common_name: Switzerland Begonia (Heirloom Bronze-Leaf Red Tuberous Begonia)

planting.note: Plant tubers hollow-side up in rich, well-drained potting mix after the danger of frost has passed.

directions: Switzerland is an heirloom tuberous begonia grown for the strong contrast between its dark bronze-green foliage and its brilliant, semi-double scarlet-red flowers, a combination that has kept it in specialty seed catalogs long after many of its contemporaries disappeared from the trade. Plant tubers hollow-side up in rich, well-drained potting mix after the danger of frost has passed, siting it where it receives bright, filtered light or a few hours of gentle morning sun, since deep shade reduces bloom and harsh afternoon sun scorches the leaves. Keep the soil evenly moist through the growing season but never waterlogged, since the fleshy tuber rots quickly in soggy conditions. In cold climates, dig and store the tuber dry over winter; in zones 9 and warmer it can be left in the ground with a protective mulch.
